summary: The nukes went off, Earth went dark, and humanity's last hope is you and up to five of your friends in a beat-up mothership full of mining ships. Cosmic Trashmen is a 2–6 player online co-op space mining game: wake up in your sleep pod, stroll to the hangar, hop into your own colour-coded ship and blast off to laser asteroids for Iron, Copper and Gold. You get 15 minutes to fill your hold, dock to cash in, and spend it all on upgrades that always come with a catch: heavier armour slows you down, a bigger cargo hold makes you breathe faster. Then the lightspeed countdown starts, and the mothership will not wait for anyone still floating out there. Run out of oxygen and you freeze solid, giving your crew 60 seconds to fly over and share their air before you're spectating for the rest of the run. Chat with proximity voice on board and crackly radio in space, where the further a friend drifts, the quieter they get. Survive three increasingly hostile jumps, from a calm asteroid field to a homing meteor shower to the scorching gas clouds of Hades, all built from real NASA asteroid and exoplanet data, and make it back to Earth with your cargo and your friendships (mostly) intact.
details: Cosmic Trashmen is our answer to the Space Mission Design Game challenge: a 2–6 player online co-op game where a crew runs a deep-space mining mission. Each player walks their mothership in first person, launches a personal mining ship, mines asteroids for ore, and docks to sell and upgrade. They must all be back aboard before a timed lightspeed jump carries the mission to its next, more dangerous destination. The game turns real mission constraints into gameplay. Oxygen, fuel, cargo mass and hull strength are limited resources. Every upgrade has a trade-off, much like a real spacecraft design budget, and stranded crewmates can only be saved by teammates who come back for them. The intended impact is to make space resource use and mission planning feel concrete and fun. Players learn that asteroids differ in composition, see real catalogued objects, and practise the communication and teamwork a real crew depends on. Every asteroid's size, rotation, brightness and spectral type comes from the NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, and spectral type decides which ore it yields. The planets and stars in each sky come from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. We built it in Unity 6 with C# and the Universal Render Pipeline. Online play uses FishNet networking over Steamworks, with Steam lobbies, party codes and invites, and Unity Vivox runs proximity voice on the ship and distance-based radio in space. The team worked through GitHub pull requests and planned on Linear. The project started in Unreal Engine 5 Blueprints, and we moved to Unity after a two-PC Steam test proved the core loop worked there. What makes it creative is the mix of friend-slop chaos and real science: a hostile, post-apocalyptic mining job built on real NASA data, where survival depends on your friends. The main factors we weighed were network reliability and scope. Ship movement runs on each player's own PC so flying feels responsive. Asteroid fields are generated from one shared seed instead of syncing hundreds of objects. Players can rejoin with their progress saved, and every feature had to pass a two-PC test with 100 ms of simulated lag and 2% packet loss. We also kept a ranked cut list so the 3-loop build could be finished on time.
